before.content_html:
A Patchwork of Living Worlds

Look at any global map of vegetation and you can see Earth’s major biomes arranged in roughly horizontal bands. Hot and wet equatorial belts hold tropical rainforests. Hot and dry zones at 30° latitude are deserts. Mid-latitudes hold temperate forests and grasslands. Cold high-latitude bands carry boreal forest (taiga) and tundra. The pattern is not coincidence: it is the product of global atmospheric circulation, ocean currents and altitude.

The Major Biomes

Edexcel asks you to know the global distribution and characteristics of seven major biomes. Tropical rainforest straddles the equator (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia) — year-round warmth, 2,000+ mm of rainfall, very high biodiversity. Temperate deciduous forest covers western Europe, eastern North America and East Asia — four seasons, 600–1,500 mm rainfall, oak/beech/maple trees. Boreal (taiga) forest circles the northern hemisphere (Siberia, Canada, Scandinavia) — cold, low rainfall, conifers like spruce and pine. Tropical grasslands (savanna) sit between rainforest and desert — wet/dry seasons, scattered trees. Temperate grasslands include the prairies and steppes — cold winters, hot summers, treeless. Hot deserts at 30° latitude (Sahara, Atacama) get under 250 mm rainfall a year. Tundra ringing the Arctic has frozen ground (permafrost) and very short summers.

Key Fact

Biomes form latitudinal bands because temperature and rainfall depend on global atmospheric circulation. Hadley-cell rising air at the equator gives rainforest; sinking air at 30° gives desert; rising Ferrel-cell air at 60° gives temperate forest; sinking Polar air gives tundra.

Why Climate Drives Distribution

Three climate factors shape biome distribution: temperature, precipitation and sunshine hours. Tropical regions are hot because the Sun’s rays strike near vertically; polar regions are cold because rays are slanted. Rainfall depends on the rising arms of circulation cells (equator, 60°) where air cools, condenses and dumps moisture. Sunshine hours influence growing seasons — Arctic summers have 24-hour daylight that lets tundra plants flower briefly.

Local Factors

Climate isn’t the only thing that matters. Altitude can recreate latitudinal patterns vertically — Mount Kilimanjaro near the equator has tropical forest at the base, alpine grassland higher up, and an icecap at the summit. Soil type: rainforest grows on poor soils because nutrients cycle quickly through living matter; deserts often have alkaline crust soils that limit plant choice. Drainage: poor drainage creates wetlands and bogs even in dry regions. Rock type: granite uplands hold acidic moorland; chalk supports calcium-loving species.

Biotic components are the living parts of a biome — plants, animals, fungi, bacteria. Abiotic components are the non-living physical parts — soil, rock, water, air, temperature, sunlight. The two are interdependent: plants need abiotic water and sunlight to grow; their decay enriches abiotic soils. Disrupt one and the other suffers — cutting tropical rainforest reduces transpiration, which reduces local rainfall, which slows regrowth.

The Biosphere as a Life-Support System

The biosphere provides goods and services to people. Goods are direct outputs: food (crops, fish, livestock), timber and fibre, medicines (a quarter of modern drugs come from rainforest plants), and fuels (firewood, biofuels). Services are less visible but vital: regulating the atmosphere’s composition (forests absorb CO₂ and release O₂), filtering water as it moves through soils and wetlands, recycling nutrients, pollinating crops, providing fresh-water storage. Without these services, modern civilisation could not function.

Key Fact

The biosphere provides goods (food, timber, medicines, fuel) and services (atmospheric regulation, water purification, pollination, nutrient cycling). The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment estimated these services are worth over $33 trillion a year — roughly the size of the entire global economy.

Indigenous and Local People

For Indigenous peoples and rural communities, the biosphere is daily life. The Yanomami of the Amazon harvest hundreds of plant species for food, medicine, building material and ritual use. The Sami of northern Scandinavia herd reindeer through the taiga. Maasai pastoralists graze cattle on East African savanna. These livelihoods depend on intact biomes and on traditional knowledge built up over centuries. Pressure on biomes — from logging, mining, climate change — threatens these communities first and most directly.

Compare three biome climate graphs side by side and the differences leap out. Equatorial rainforest: a flat, high temperature line at 25–28°C; high rainfall (200+ mm) every month. Hot desert: a wide temperature swing (5°C nights to 45°C days), almost no rainfall in any month. Tundra: temperatures below freezing for most of the year, with a brief summer above zero; very low rainfall, mostly as snow. Identifying biomes from climate graphs is a regular exam task — practise pattern recognition.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Explain question on biome distribution, link climate to circulation cells. The right answer goes ‘rainforests cluster on the equator (location) because the Hadley cell rises here (process), bringing year-round heavy rainfall (cause) which supports lush evergreen forest (effect)’. Naming circulation cells lifts a 2-mark answer to 4. Examiners reward precise terms like biotic, abiotic, biosphere and ecosystem services.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following biomes has the highest annual rainfall?
A) Tropical rainforest
B) Hot desert
C) Tundra
D) Temperate grassland
practice_questions.marks: A) Tropical rainforest. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'biome'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A large-scale ecosystem found around the world that shares similar climate, plants and animals, such as tropical rainforest or tundra.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A type of ecosystem like rainforest or desert.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of hot deserts.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: located around 30°N and 30°S latitude; on the western sides of continents; named examples — Sahara (North Africa), Arabian, Australian, Atacama (South America), Sonoran (North America). Mastering: latitude pattern + 2 named examples. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain why tropical rainforests are found near the equator.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: equator receives the most direct and intense sunlight, so air heats and rises (Hadley cell rising arm); rising air cools, condenses and produces year-round heavy rainfall; constant high temperatures (25–28°C) plus 2,000+ mm rainfall create perfect conditions for evergreen forest; high biodiversity follows. Mastering: full chain from sunlight → circulation → rainfall → vegetation. [4]

practice_questions.text: A tropical rainforest receives 2,400 mm of rainfall a year. Calculate the average monthly rainfall. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 2,400 ÷ 12 = 200 mm/month. Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: 200 mm with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]
Emerging: tries division. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine how local factors modify the broad pattern of biomes shaped by global climate.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: altitude — Mount Kilimanjaro shows tropical/alpine/icecap zones at one location; soil — rainforest grows on poor soils with rapid nutrient cycling; drainage — wetlands form even in dry regions; rock type — granite gives acidic moorland; ocean currents — Atacama desert exists on a tropical coast because cold Humboldt current suppresses rainfall. Conclusion: latitude/circulation set the broad pattern but local factors create regional and altitudinal variations. Mastering (7–8): 3+ factors with named examples.

lessons.title: Demand on the Biosphere: Food, Water & Energy

before.content_html:
Why Is Demand on the Biosphere Rising?

Every meal you eat, every glass of water you drink and every device you charge depends on the biosphere. As the world’s population grows and lifestyles change, the pressure on these natural systems is climbing fast. The enquiry running through this lesson is simple but urgent — can the biosphere keep providing food, water and energy for everyone, or will demand outstrip what the planet can renew?

Four forces are driving demand upwards. First, population growth: from 2.5 billion in 1950, the world reached 8 billion in 2022 and is projected to peak near 10 billion around 2080. Second, rising affluence — as countries become wealthier, diets shift towards meat and dairy, which require far more land and water per calorie than grains. Third, urbanisation — cities now hold over 56% of people and use vast amounts of energy and water. Fourth, industrialisation — emerging economies like India and Indonesia are building factories that depend on fossil fuels and minerals.

Key Fact

Demand on the biosphere is rising due to population growth, rising affluence, urbanisation and industrialisation. Together they push food, water and energy use to record highs.

Demand for Food

The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates global food demand will be 60% higher in 2050 than it was in 2010. Two changes drive this. More mouths, of course — an extra two billion people. But also dietary transition: as China’s middle class expanded, average meat consumption rose from 13 kg per person in 1980 to over 60 kg today. Producing one kilogram of beef takes around 15,000 litres of water and far more land than a kilogram of wheat. So as wealth rises, so does the land and water bill of every meal.

Demand for Water

Around 70% of all freshwater used by humans goes to agriculture — especially for crops like rice and cotton, and for the grain fed to livestock. Industry takes another 20%, and households the rest. Water demand is rising twice as fast as population because of meat-rich diets, more factories and longer showers in wealthier homes. The result is water stress: parts of northern China, the western United States, North Africa and South Asia already pump groundwater faster than rain can refill it.

In 1960 the Aral Sea, on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the world’s fourth-largest lake. Soviet planners diverted its two feeder rivers to irrigate cotton fields. By 2014 the eastern lobe had dried up completely. Fishing communities collapsed, dust storms now carry pesticide-laden sand across the region, and infant mortality in nearby villages rose sharply. The Aral Sea is the textbook example of human demand outrunning what the biosphere can supply.

Demand for Energy

Global energy use has more than doubled since 1980 and the International Energy Agency expects another 25% rise by 2040. Most of that extra demand comes from emerging economies: China overtook the United States as the world’s largest energy consumer in 2009 and India is on track to do the same by 2030. Households want lighting, fridges, air conditioning and electric vehicles. Factories want electricity for steel, cement and chemicals. Currently about 80% of energy comes from fossil fuels, so rising demand also means rising carbon emissions and pressure on forests and oceans.

Key Fact

Around 70% of freshwater is used by farming, 20% by industry and 10% by households. Meat-rich diets and industrialisation push agricultural and industrial water demand up the fastest.

Malthus — The Pessimist

Two opposing theories try to explain what happens when population meets resources. In 1798, the English clergyman Thomas Malthus argued that population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8…) while food supply only grows arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4…). Sooner or later population must outrun food, causing famine, disease or war — what he called ‘positive checks’. Modern Malthusians (or neo-Malthusians) point to droughts, fisheries collapse and rising food prices as evidence that the theory still applies. Critics argue Malthus was wrong in 1798 — food supply has grown far faster than he predicted — but right that any finite planet must have limits.

Boserup — The Optimist

In 1965 the Danish economist Ester Boserup turned Malthus on his head. She argued that necessity is the mother of invention: when population pressure rises, people invent new technologies and farming methods to feed themselves. Examples include the medieval shift from two-field to three-field crop rotation; the Green Revolution from the 1960s, when high-yield wheat and rice varieties tripled output in India and Mexico; and modern precision agriculture using GPS-guided tractors and drip irrigation. For Boserup, demand drives progress — not collapse.

The honest answer is ‘both, and it depends’. Boserup looks correct globally — humans have fed nearly five times as many people as in 1900. But Malthus looks correct regionally: Yemen, Somalia and parts of the Sahel face recurring food crises where population growth, climate stress and conflict have outrun local food supply. Innovation also has costs — the Green Revolution doubled yields but contaminated groundwater with fertilisers and made farmers dependent on imported seeds. The bigger question is whether innovation can keep pace with climate change, which is reducing yields in many tropical regions.

Population projections from the UN now suggest world population will plateau, not explode, peaking somewhere between 9.5 and 10.5 billion by 2080. That gives a window for technology to keep up — but only if energy, food and water systems are reformed. The next lessons explore one of the biosphere’s most stressed regions: tropical rainforests and the taiga, where rising demand is colliding with fragile ecosystems.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Explain question on rising demand, examiners want named drivers (population, affluence, urbanisation, industrialisation) AND specific evidence — rising Chinese meat consumption, water stress in northern China, energy demand projections. For 8-mark Examine questions on Malthus and Boserup, always frame your answer as a debate. State both positions, weigh the evidence (Aral Sea vs Green Revolution), and reach a justified conclusion. Don’t simply summarise the theories.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a driver of rising demand on the biosphere?
A) Population growth
B) Urbanisation
C) Falling life expectancy
D) Industrialisation
practice_questions.marks: C) Falling life expectancy. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'water stress'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A situation where demand for water in a region exceeds the amount available, even when rainfall may be adequate, often caused by overuse of groundwater or irrigation.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'When there isn't enough water to meet demand.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways rising affluence increases pressure on the biosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Wealthier people eat more meat and dairy, which use much more land and water per calorie than grain crops.
• Higher incomes mean more cars, larger homes, air conditioning and frequent flying — all raising energy and resource use.
• Wealthier consumers replace electronics and clothes more often, raising demand for minerals and water.
Mastering: two clear ways with development and named example (e.g. Chinese meat consumption rising from 13 kg to 60 kg per capita). [3]
Secure: two ways named with brief explanation. [2]
Developing: one way named, weak development. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Malthus and Boserup differ in their views on population and resources.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Malthus (1798) argued population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so population must outrun food, leading to famine, disease or war (positive checks).
• Boserup (1965) argued the opposite — population pressure drives innovation: new farming methods and technologies raise output to match demand.
• Malthus is essentially pessimistic; Boserup essentially optimistic.
• Both can be illustrated — Malthus through famines in the Sahel, Boserup through the Green Revolution.
Mastering: clear contrast between both theories with named example for each. [4]
Secure: both theories accurately stated with one example. [3]

practice_questions.text: World population was around 2.5 billion in 1950 and is projected to peak at about 10 billion by 2080. Calculate the percentage increase in population from 1950 to the projected peak. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 10 − 2.5 = 7.5 billion; percentage increase = (7.5 ÷ 2.5) × 100 = 300%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 300% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the view that Boserup's theory better explains today's relationship between population and resources than Malthus's theory.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Arguments supporting Boserup:
• Global food output has grown faster than population since 1960, thanks to the Green Revolution, GM crops and precision agriculture.
• Population is projected to plateau near 10 billion, not explode — demographic transition is reducing growth in many countries.
• Innovations like drip irrigation, vertical farming and lab-grown meat suggest more solutions are coming.
Arguments supporting Malthus:
• Around 750 million people remain undernourished — demand is outrunning local food supply in places like Yemen and the Sahel.
• The Aral Sea collapse, depleted aquifers in northern China and the western US, and overfishing in the North Atlantic show resource limits.
• Climate change is already reducing yields in tropical regions, suggesting innovation may not keep pace.
Mastering (7-8): balanced examination, specific evidence on both sides, reasoned conclusion (e.g. Boserup is correct globally, Malthus regionally). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both theories examined with some specific evidence and a conclusion. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one theory examined more thoroughly, limited evidence. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): theories described not examined, no clear conclusion. [1-2]
SPaG (4): consistently accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with confident use of specialist terms. [4]

before.content_html:
Why Are Tropical Rainforests Special?

Tropical rainforests cover only about 6% of the Earth’s surface but contain more than half of all known land species. They sit in a belt around the equator — the Amazon, the Congo and parts of Southeast Asia — where temperatures stay between 25°C and 30°C and rainfall exceeds 2,000 mm a year. Constant warmth and moisture create the most productive ecosystem on Earth: lush, layered, and humming with life. The enquiry for this lesson is what allows the rainforest to function so spectacularly — and why those same systems are so easily disrupted.

The Layered Structure

A rainforest works in vertical stories. The emergent layer rises 40–55 metres above the ground — tall hardwoods like the kapok tree poke through the canopy, exposed to the most sun and wind. The canopy at 30–45 metres forms a dense roof that captures most of the light and is home to perhaps 70% of rainforest species. Below that is the cooler, darker understorey of saplings and shrubs, and a thin forest floor where leaf litter is broken down within weeks by termites, fungi and bacteria.

Key Fact

Rainforests have four vertical layers — emergent (40–55 m), canopy (30–45 m), understorey, and forest floor. Most species and most photosynthesis happen in the canopy.

Plant and Animal Adaptations

Plants and animals are finely adapted to the climate. Drip-tip leaves shed heavy rain quickly to stop fungus growing on the leaf surface. Buttress roots — huge above-ground supports that flare out from the trunk — stabilise tall trees in shallow soil. Lianas climb other trees to reach the sunlight. Many animals are arboreal — sloths, spider monkeys, toucans — with adaptations like prehensile tails, strong limbs and bright colours that help them communicate or camouflage among the leaves. Frogs lay their eggs in pools of rainwater trapped in bromeliads — tiny ecosystems within the canopy.

The rainforest’s nutrient store is held mostly in the living trees, not the soil. Leaves, fruits and dead animals fall to the floor and are decomposed within weeks by warm, moist air full of fungi and insects. Nutrients are taken up almost immediately by shallow roots and recycled into new growth. The nutrient cycle here is fast and tight; remove the trees and the system collapses, because the soil itself holds little. This is why deforested land becomes infertile within a few years.

A Complex Food Web

Energy flows through a rainforest in a dense food web. Producers (trees, lianas, ferns) capture solar energy through photosynthesis. Primary consumers eat them — insects, sloths, monkeys. Secondary consumers like jaguars, anacondas and harpy eagles eat the herbivores. Decomposers break everything down. The web is dense because there are so many species: lose one and others can usually take its place. But lose a keystone species — like a top predator or a fig tree that feeds dozens of birds — and a chain reaction can ripple through the whole system.

Key Fact

Rainforests have high biodiversity, fast nutrient cycling and complex food webs. Most nutrients are stored in the living trees, not the soil — making cleared land surprisingly poor for long-term farming.

Direct Threats: Deforestation

Deforestation is the biggest direct threat. The Amazon has lost around 20% of its area since 1970. Six causes drive most of the clearance. Commercial agriculture — cattle ranching in Brazil, palm oil plantations in Indonesia, soybean fields for animal feed — takes the largest single share. Subsistence farming using slash-and-burn methods clears smaller patches that often degrade after a few harvests. Hardwood logging for mahogany and teak removes the largest trees. Fuel wood collection by local people thins the forest. Mining for iron ore, bauxite and gold (in places like Carajás and Yanomami territory) strips and pollutes large areas. HEP dams, like the Belo Monte project in Brazil, flood huge tracts to generate electricity, displacing communities and clearing more access roads.

Indirect Threats: Climate Change

Climate change is an indirect but rising threat. Hotter, drier conditions cause ecosystem stress: trees shed leaves, growth slows, and pests and diseases spread further. The Amazon experienced unusual droughts in 2005, 2010 and 2015–16 which caused tree die-back and triggered enormous wildfires — ironic, because rainforests are normally too damp to burn. There is a tipping point: scientists warn that if 25% of the Amazon is lost, the whole forest could shift from absorbing carbon dioxide to releasing it, accelerating climate change globally. Around 17–20% has already been lost.

Tropical rainforests are sometimes called the ‘lungs of the planet’. They store an estimated 200 billion tonnes of carbon, regulate the global hydrological cycle by releasing water vapour, and house species that supply 25% of modern medicines (including treatments derived from the rosy periwinkle for childhood leukaemia). Their loss damages indigenous people directly — tribes such as the Yanomami face threats from miners and disease — but also affects everyone through climate, weather and food prices.

The next lesson looks north, to a very different kind of forest — the cold, slow-growing taiga of Siberia, Canada and Scandinavia — and asks why it is now under pressure too.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Explain question on deforestation causes, examiners want at least two distinct causes (e.g. commercial agriculture AND HEP dams) with named places — Brazil’s soya belt, Belo Monte dam, Indonesian palm oil. Avoid saying ‘deforestation is bad’ without explanation. For nutrient-cycle questions, draw or describe the rapid leaf litter → decomposition → root-uptake loop. For climate-change indirect threat questions, link drought to wildfires to tipping point.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a direct threat to tropical rainforests?
A) Climate change causing drought
B) Cattle ranching expansion in Brazil
C) Atmospheric CO2 rising globally
D) Increasing world population
practice_questions.marks: B) Cattle ranching expansion in Brazil. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'nutrient cycle'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The continuous movement of nutrients between living plants, animals, leaf litter and soil within an ecosystem, where decomposition releases nutrients that are reabsorbed by plant roots.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'How nutrients move between plants, animals and soil.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two adaptations that allow rainforest trees to survive in hot, wet conditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Drip-tip leaves shed heavy rain quickly so fungus does not grow on the leaf surface, keeping photosynthesis efficient.
• Buttress roots flare out from the trunk to stabilise tall trees in the shallow forest soil.
• Tall, straight trunks reach light at the canopy level.
• Smooth bark allows climbing plants and rainwater to slide off easily.
Mastering: two adaptations clearly described with explanation of purpose. [3]
Secure: two adaptations named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how climate change acts as an indirect threat to tropical rainforests.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Higher temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns cause ecosystem stress: trees grow more slowly and shed leaves earlier.
• Drought makes the forest dry enough to burn — Amazon droughts in 2005, 2010 and 2015–16 led to widespread fires.
• Pests and diseases spread further as warmer climates allow them to survive in places they could not before.
• If around 25% of the Amazon is lost, scientists warn of a tipping point where the forest releases more carbon than it absorbs.
Mastering: clear chain of cause and effect with named example (e.g. 2010 Amazon drought). [4]
Secure: two effects explained with reference to climate. [3]

practice_questions.text: A satellite image shows that 18,000 km² of Amazon rainforest was cleared in one year, while in the previous year 10,000 km² was cleared. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 18,000 − 10,000 = 8,000 km²; percentage increase = (8,000 ÷ 10,000) × 100 = 80%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 80% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the threats to tropical rainforests, considering both direct and indirect causes of damage.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Direct threats:
• Commercial agriculture (cattle ranching, soya, palm oil) is the largest cause; Brazilian Amazon clearance is mostly driven by beef and soy exports.
• Hardwood logging removes mahogany and teak, often illegally.
• Mining (iron ore in Carajás, gold in Yanomami territory) strips land and pollutes rivers.
• HEP dams like Belo Monte flood large areas and require new roads, which open further forest to settlers.
• Subsistence farming using slash-and-burn clears smaller patches and uses up nutrients.
Indirect threats:
• Climate change causes drought, ecosystem stress and wildfires (Amazon 2005, 2010, 2015–16).
• Pests and diseases spread further into stressed forests.
• Demand-side pressure: rich-country consumers create export demand for beef, soya and palm oil.
Mastering (7-8): both direct and indirect threats examined with named examples and a clear judgement on which is more serious or how they interact. [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both types covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one type fully covered, other only mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination, no examples. [1-2]
SPaG (4): consistently accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with confident use of specialist terms. [4]

before.content_html:
A Forest Around the Top of the World

The taiga — sometimes called boreal forest — forms the largest land biome on Earth, ringing the planet across northern Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska. Where the rainforest is hot, wet and bursting with life, the taiga is cold, slow and quiet. Winters drop to −30°C or below; summers are short and cool, with growing seasons of just three to four months. This lesson asks why a forest so vast and so cold is now under increasing pressure.

Climate and Soils

Taiga rainfall is modest — 300 to 800 mm a year — mostly falling as snow. Beneath much of it lies permafrost: ground that stays frozen all year, thawing only in a thin top layer for a few weeks in summer. Soils are thin, acidic and slow to form because cold air slows decomposition. Pine needles drop and lie on the floor for years, often called ‘needle litter’, before fungi can break them down. Compared with the rainforest’s rapid recycling, the taiga’s nutrient cycle is sluggish and locked up.

Key Fact

Taiga has a short growing season (3–4 months), thin acidic soils and slow nutrient cycling. Permafrost beneath the surface limits root depth and water drainage.

Plant Adaptations

Most taiga trees are coniferous evergreens — pines, spruces and firs — with adaptations matched to the climate. Their cone shape sheds heavy snow without breaking branches. Needles instead of broad leaves cut water loss and have a waxy coating that resists frost. Being evergreen means trees can photosynthesise the moment the brief summer arrives, without wasting time growing new leaves. Roots are shallow and wide because they cannot push through the permafrost. Mosses and lichens, not flowering plants, dominate the forest floor.

Animal Adaptations

Taiga animals are adapted to cold and seasonal scarcity. Brown bears hibernate through winter, surviving on stored fat. Many caribou and birds migrate south to escape the worst weather. Year-round residents like the lynx, wolverine and snowshoe hare grow thick fur or feathers and switch to white winter coats for camouflage in snow. Biodiversity is much lower than the rainforest — perhaps a few hundred mammal and bird species for the whole biome — because the conditions are too harsh for many specialised forms.

Productivity — the rate at which the ecosystem produces new living matter — is roughly one-tenth that of a rainforest. Three reasons: short growing season; cold soils that slow microbial activity, so nutrients do not return to plants quickly; and a low-light angle for much of the year. Once a taiga tree is felled, it can take 80–150 years for a new tree of the same size to grow back. That makes the forest unusually vulnerable to over-exploitation.

Direct Threats: Logging and Energy

The taiga’s threats are different from those facing the rainforest. The biggest direct threat is softwood logging: pine and spruce are felled for paper pulp, packaging and construction timber. Russia, Canada and Sweden are among the world’s largest exporters. Indirectly, demand for fossil fuels and minerals opens up isolated regions: Alberta’s tar sands operations clear forests to mine bitumen; Russia’s Yamal Peninsula has been criss-crossed by gas pipelines; northern Quebec has new HEP dams on rivers like La Grande, flooding tens of thousands of square kilometres. Once roads, pipelines and dam reservoirs reach a remote area, settlers and further industry usually follow.

Key Fact

The taiga’s main commercial threats are softwood logging (Russia, Canada, Sweden), fossil fuels (Canadian tar sands, Russian gas), mining (nickel, copper, gold), and HEP dams (Quebec, Russia).

Indirect Threats: Acid Rain, Pests and Fire

Acid precipitation from coal-burning power stations and smelters has damaged taiga forests for decades. The Sudbury smelter in Ontario killed thousands of square kilometres of forest before pollution controls were tightened. Warmer winters allow pests like the spruce bark beetle to survive and multiply: in British Columbia, beetles have killed about half of the merchantable lodgepole pine since the 1990s — an area larger than England. Climate change is also lengthening fire seasons. Russian taiga fires in 2019 burned an area roughly the size of Belgium; California-style mega-fires now reach as far north as Alaska. Fires release stored carbon into the atmosphere, accelerating warming further.

The taiga and its frozen soils together store more carbon than any other land biome on Earth — perhaps twice as much as the rainforests. As permafrost thaws and fires release stored carbon, the taiga risks switching from a long-term carbon sink to a major emissions source. This is one reason the taiga matters far beyond its boundaries: damage here threatens the global climate system itself.

The next lesson turns to solutions. Faced with both rainforest deforestation and taiga over-exploitation, what global actions and sustainable management strategies are working — and which are failing?

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes the taiga's growing season?
options: Only 3 to 4 months because of the cold climate
All year because of mild conditions
Around 9 months as in temperate forests
Only summer days at the equator

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of tree dominates the taiga?
options: Coniferous evergreens such as pine and spruce

knowledge_checks.q: _____ is permanently frozen ground that thaws only in a thin layer in summer.
_____ precipitation forms when sulphur and nitrogen oxides mix with rainwater.
Match each taiga threat to its main category:

flashcard_questions.a: The vast belt of cold-climate coniferous forest stretching across northern Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a typical adaptation of taiga trees?
A) Needle-shaped leaves
B) Cone-shaped crown
C) Buttress roots
D) Waxy leaf coating
practice_questions.marks: C) Buttress roots. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'permafrost'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Ground that remains frozen throughout the year, with only the top thin active layer thawing during the short summer.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Ground that stays frozen.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways that taiga animals are adapted to long, cold winters.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Some animals (brown bears, ground squirrels) hibernate through winter, living off body fat.
• Many birds and caribou migrate south for winter, returning in spring.
• Year-round residents (lynx, snowshoe hare) grow thick fur or feathers and switch to white coats for camouflage in snow.
• Some store food during the brief summer (squirrels caching pine cones).
Mastering: two adaptations clearly described, with reason. [3]
Secure: two adaptations named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how acid precipitation damages taiga ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Acid rain forms when sulphur and nitrogen oxides from coal-burning and smelting mix with water in the atmosphere.
• When it falls on the taiga it lowers soil pH, killing soil bacteria and damaging fine roots, so trees absorb fewer nutrients.
• Acidic water enters lakes and streams, killing fish eggs and disrupting food chains.
• Around the Sudbury nickel smelter in Ontario, thousands of square kilometres of forest died before pollution controls were tightened.
Mastering: clear cause-effect chain with named example (Sudbury). [4]
Secure: two effects explained. [3]

practice_questions.text: A taiga forest reserve covers 60,000 km². Wildfire destroyed 9,000 km² in one summer. Calculate the percentage of the reserve lost. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: percentage = (9,000 ÷ 60,000) × 100 = 15%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 15% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the threats facing the taiga today, considering both commercial development and climate-related factors.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Commercial development:
• Softwood logging for paper pulp and construction (Russia, Canada, Sweden).
• Fossil fuel extraction — Alberta tar sands clear forest to mine bitumen; Russian Yamal Peninsula gas pipelines.
• Mining for nickel, copper and gold scars and pollutes the landscape.
• HEP dams in Quebec and Russia flood tens of thousands of square kilometres.
Climate-related factors:
• Acid precipitation has killed forest around Sudbury, Ontario.
• Spruce bark beetle outbreaks in British Columbia killed half the merchantable lodgepole pine since the 1990s.
• Russian taiga wildfires in 2019 burned an area the size of Belgium, releasing stored carbon and worsening warming.
• Permafrost thaw threatens long-term carbon storage.
Mastering (7-8): both categories examined with named examples and a reasoned conclusion (e.g. fires and pests now match logging in scale). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both categories covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one category covered well, other mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination. [1-2]
SPaG (4): consistently accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with confident use of specialist terms. [4]

before.content_html:
Can Forests Be Protected?

Tropical rainforests and the taiga both face heavy pressure, but they are not lost causes. Across the world, governments, NGOs and indigenous communities are experimenting with ways to save what is left while still allowing people to make a living. The question this lesson explores is whether global agreements and sustainable management actually work — or whether they only slow the loss.

Global Action: CITES

Signed in 1973 and now ratified by 184 countries, CITES regulates the international trade in endangered plant and animal species. Mahogany, rosewood and ramin — valuable rainforest hardwoods — are listed, meaning exports require special permits. Animal trade controls cover orangutans, jaguars and parrots. CITES has reduced trade in some species (the global ivory ban cut elephant poaching sharply in some countries) but enforcement is patchy — illegal logging and wildlife smuggling remain billion-pound criminal industries. CITES works best when wealthy importing countries also commit to inspections at customs.

Global Action: REDD

The UN’s REDD programme — Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation — pays developing countries to keep forests standing rather than cutting them down. Norway has pledged hundreds of millions of dollars to Brazil and Indonesia under REDD-style agreements. The logic is straightforward: forests store carbon, so paying for that storage is cheaper than building expensive carbon-capture technology. Critics argue REDD can be undermined by weak monitoring (some payments have gone to areas that were never threatened) and by political change — Brazil’s deforestation rates jumped under President Bolsonaro from 2019, despite earlier REDD progress.

Key Fact

CITES regulates trade in endangered species. REDD pays developing countries to keep forests standing for carbon storage. CITES uses laws and bans; REDD uses cash incentives.

Why Some Areas Are Improving and Others Are Not

Deforestation rates are not the same everywhere. Costa Rica has reversed forest loss: payments to landowners for environmental services and the growth of ecotourism mean tree cover has risen from 26% in the 1980s to over 50% today. Indonesia has slowed but not reversed loss after a 2019 moratorium on new palm-oil licences. Brazil cut Amazon deforestation by roughly 80% between 2004 and 2012 through enforcement, satellite monitoring and the Soy Moratorium — an agreement among soy traders not to buy from newly cleared land. But progress can be reversed by politics: 2019–2022 saw a sharp rise again before tougher rules returned in 2023.

In 2006, after pressure from Greenpeace and supermarket chains, the largest grain traders agreed not to buy soya beans from any land in the Brazilian Amazon cleared after a fixed cut-off date. Satellite monitoring and farm registration made it work. By 2014, soy expansion accounted for less than 1% of new Amazon deforestation, down from over 30%. The lesson: when consumer demand, traders and government enforcement align, a market-led ban can work fast.

Sustainable Forest Management

Even forests that are used commercially can be managed sustainably. Selective logging takes only mature trees of certain species, leaving the rest of the canopy intact. Replanting with native species (rather than monoculture plantations) restores ecological function. The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certifies wood products from forests managed to strict environmental and social standards — FSC labels appear on garden furniture, paper and books in UK shops, telling consumers their purchase has not driven deforestation. In the taiga, FSC has helped persuade Swedish and Canadian companies to spare old-growth forest and leave wildlife corridors between cuts.

Alternative Livelihoods

Long-term protection only works if local people can earn a living from a standing forest. Ecotourism takes visitors into rainforest reserves with trained local guides; Costa Rica’s Monteverde Cloud Forest reserve generates millions of dollars a year and employs hundreds of people. Sustainable farming on the forest edge — agroforestry, shade-grown coffee, smallholder cacao — gives families an income without further clearance. Indigenous land rights matter too: studies show forests under indigenous management have lower deforestation rates than even most national parks. The Yanomami in Brazil and the Sami in northern Sweden are pushing for stronger legal recognition for this reason.

Key Fact

Sustainable management means selective logging, replanting and FSC certification. Alternative livelihoods — ecotourism, agroforestry, shade-grown coffee — let people earn from forests without destroying them.

The taiga is harder to protect because it is so vast and so remote. National parks like Wood Buffalo (Canada) and the protected wilderness of northern Sweden conserve large blocks of old-growth boreal forest. Sustainable forestry — longer rotation cycles of 80–120 years, leaving wildlife corridors and old standing trees — is increasingly required in Sweden and Finland. But conflicting views remain: indigenous communities want full protection, governments often back logging and oil revenue, and conservationists push for wilderness reserves. Compromises usually allow some commercial use while protecting the most ecologically valuable areas.

No single tool will save the world’s forests. The combination that works — international agreements like CITES and REDD, market pressure from supermarkets, FSC labelling, satellite enforcement and local livelihoods — is messy but increasingly effective where it is taken seriously.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Explain question on forest management, examiners want named strategies (CITES, REDD, FSC) PLUS a specific outcome (Brazil’s soy moratorium dropped clearance from 30% to 1%, Costa Rica’s tree cover rose from 26% to over 50%). For 8-mark Examine questions, weigh advantages against disadvantages: REDD pays for storage but is undermined by political change. Use named places — vague answers about ‘developing countries’ lose marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the main purpose of CITES?
A) To pay countries to plant new forests
B) To regulate the international trade in endangered plant and animal species
C) To certify wood products as sustainable
D) To organise rainforest ecotourism trips
practice_questions.marks: B) To regulate the international trade in endangered plant and animal species. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ecotourism'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Tourism that focuses on undisturbed natural areas and is designed to be low-impact, with money raised funding conservation and local livelihoods.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Tourism in natural areas that helps protect them.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a forest can be managed sustainably.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Selective logging — only mature trees of certain species are cut, leaving the rest of the canopy intact for regeneration.
• Replanting with native species rather than monoculture plantations to restore ecological function.
• FSC certification — independent verification that a forest is managed to strict environmental and social standards.
• Longer rotation cycles in the taiga (80–120 years) leaving wildlife corridors.
Mastering: two strategies clearly described. [3]
Secure: two strategies named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Brazilian soy moratorium reduced deforestation in the Amazon.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In 2006, the largest grain traders agreed not to buy soya beans from any Amazon land cleared after a fixed cut-off date.
• Satellite monitoring and farm registration made it possible to track which farms had cleared forest illegally.
• Supermarkets and consumers pressured traders, lining up market demand with conservation rules.
• Result: soy expansion fell from over 30% of new Amazon deforestation to under 1% by 2014.
Mastering: clear cause-effect chain with quantified outcome. [4]
Secure: process explained with one piece of data. [3]

practice_questions.text: Costa Rica's forest cover rose from 26% of the country in the 1980s to 52% today. Calculate the percentage point increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 52 − 26 = 26 percentage points. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 26 with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the view that global agreements like CITES and REDD have been more effective than local actions in protecting forests.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Arguments supporting global agreements:
• CITES has cut trade in endangered species; the global ivory ban reduced elephant poaching sharply in some countries.
• REDD payments helped Brazil reduce Amazon deforestation by 80% between 2004 and 2012, with Norwegian funding.
• International rules can pressure governments and TNCs that local communities cannot.
Arguments supporting local actions:
• Indigenous-managed forests show lower clearance rates than many national parks.
• The Brazilian soy moratorium — a market-led local agreement — cut soy-driven deforestation from 30% to 1%.
• Costa Rica's national tree-cover policy and ecotourism raised forest cover from 26% to over 50%.
• Local FSC-certified forestry and Sami land claims show that strong local action protects specific places effectively.
Mastering (7-8): both global and local examined with named examples and a balanced judgement (e.g. global agreements work best when paired with local enforcement). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one covered well, other only mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination. [1-2]
SPaG (4): consistently accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with confident use of specialist terms. [4]

before.content_html:
Three Kinds of Energy

Modern life runs on energy — for lighting, transport, factories, heating and the internet. Energy resources fall into three groups. Non-renewable resources are finite stocks of fossil fuels: coal, oil and natural gas, formed from buried organic matter over hundreds of millions of years. Once burned they are gone for our purposes. Renewable resources flow continuously from the natural environment: solar, wind and hydroelectric power (HEP). They will not run out on human timescales. Recyclable resources sit between the two: nuclear fuel can be reprocessed, and biofuels (ethanol from sugar cane, biodiesel from rapeseed) regrow if managed sustainably.

Key Fact

Energy resources are non-renewable (coal, oil, gas), renewable (solar, wind, HEP) or recyclable (nuclear, biofuels). Around 80% of world energy still comes from fossil fuels.

Environmental Costs of Extraction

All energy carries an environmental cost. Mining coal scars the landscape and produces acidic waste water; the Appalachian region in the United States lost mountain tops to surface mining. Drilling for oil risks spills — the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill in the Gulf of Mexico released around 4.9 million barrels and killed marine wildlife from Louisiana to Florida. Burning fossil fuels emits CO₂, the largest cause of climate change. Renewables are not impact-free either: HEP dams like China’s Three Gorges flooded ancient towns and displaced 1.3 million people. Wind farms use large areas of countryside and can affect bird flight paths. Solar farms need cleared land. The trade-offs are unavoidable, but renewables emit far less CO₂ over their lifetime.

Why Access Varies

Access to energy is not evenly distributed. Three factors shape what countries can use. Physical resources: oil-rich countries like Saudi Arabia and Norway sit on huge reserves; sunny countries like Spain and Morocco have strong solar potential; mountainous countries like Norway and Switzerland have ideal HEP terrain. The UK has comparatively poor solar but excellent offshore wind because of its windy continental shelf. Geology and accessibility: oil and gas are hard to extract from deep ocean or remote Arctic basins. Technology and capital: high-tech extraction (deep-water drilling, nuclear) needs wealthy economies. Rich countries can also import what they lack — the UK imports gas from Norway and the United States.

A world map of energy resources shows clear clusters. The Persian Gulf and Russia hold most of the world’s oil and gas. China and Australia hold massive coal reserves. The sunniest solar belt runs through North Africa, the Middle East, the southwest United States, Australia and northern Chile. The best wind potential lies offshore in the North Sea, off Cape Horn and along the Patagonian coast. HEP is dominated by China, Brazil and Canada because of their long fast-flowing rivers. Reading these maps tells you which countries hold geopolitical leverage and which depend on imports.

Energy Use Per Capita

Energy use per person varies enormously. The United States uses around 78,000 kWh of total energy per person per year; the UK around 32,000; India around 6,000; Ethiopia under 1,000. Three causes drive these gaps. Economic development: wealthy economies have more cars, larger homes, factories and electronic devices. Reliance on traditional fuels: in low-income countries, hundreds of millions still cook on wood, charcoal or dung — counted as ‘energy use’ only loosely, but a major source of indoor air pollution. Sectoral mix: countries with heavy industry (steel, cement, chemicals) use far more energy per unit of GDP than service-led economies. Norway and Iceland have unusually high per capita figures because of energy-intensive aluminium smelters powered by HEP.

Key Fact

Energy use per capita rises sharply with development — the average American uses 13 times more energy than the average Indian. Industry, transport and household appliances are the largest users.

Why Oil Demand Keeps Rising

Energy security — reliable, affordable supply — is a major political concern. Oil sits at the centre of the global economy: it powers most cars, lorries, ships and aircraft, and is the raw material for plastics and fertilisers. Demand keeps rising mainly because emerging economies are buying more vehicles. China overtook the United States as the world’s largest car market in 2009; India’s middle class is repeating the pattern now. Per capita GDP and per capita oil use have moved closely together in every fast-industrialising country since 1950.

Oil Supply: Concentrated and Political

Oil reserves are unevenly distributed. About half lie in the Middle East — Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates. Russia, Venezuela, the United States and Canada hold most of the rest. Twelve major exporters coordinate through OPEC (the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries) which can raise or cut production to influence prices. Conflict shifts supply: the 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled global prices in months; the 1990 Gulf War, the 2003 Iraq invasion and the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine all caused price spikes. Economic cycles matter too: the 2008 financial crisis cut prices from $147 to $40 a barrel as demand collapsed; the COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020 briefly drove US prices below zero.

An oil price graph from 1970 to today shows huge spikes and crashes. Spikes line up with conflict (1973 embargo, 1979 Iranian revolution, 2022 Ukraine invasion). Crashes match recessions (1980s glut, 2008 financial crisis, 2020 pandemic). Long-run trend has been upwards as demand from emerging economies has grown faster than new supply has come online. Examiners reward students who pair specific events with specific price moves — vague answers about ‘going up and down’ lose marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a recyclable energy resource?
A) Natural gas
B) Wind power
C) Coal
D) Nuclear fuel
practice_questions.marks: D) Nuclear fuel. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'energy security'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A condition where a country has reliable, affordable and sufficient energy supplies, ideally with a diversified mix of sources to reduce vulnerability to disruption.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Having enough energy supply for a country.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why per-capita energy use varies between countries.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic development: wealthier countries have more cars, larger homes, more appliances and heavy industry, all of which raise energy use.
• Reliance on traditional fuels: in poorer countries, many households still cook with wood or charcoal which is only loosely measured.
• Sectoral mix: countries with energy-intensive industries (steel, aluminium, cement) use more energy per unit of GDP than service-led economies.
• Climate: cold countries use more for heating, hot countries for air conditioning.
Mastering: two clear reasons with country examples. [3]
Secure: two reasons named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how political conflict can affect oil supply and prices.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Conflicts in oil-producing regions cut supply: the 1973 Arab oil embargo restricted exports to the West and quadrupled prices in months.
• Wars disrupt shipping routes: 1990 Gulf War, 2003 Iraq invasion and 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine all caused price spikes.
• Sanctions on oil exporters (e.g. Russia after 2022) force buyers to pay more elsewhere.
• OPEC countries can also choose to cut production for political reasons.
Mastering: clear cause-effect chain with specific dates and named events. [4]
Secure: two effects explained with one named event. [3]

practice_questions.text: An oil price graph shows that oil rose from $40 a barrel in early 2008 to $147 a barrel by July, then fell back to $40 by December. Calculate the percentage increase from January to July. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = $147 − $40 = $107; percentage increase = ($107 ÷ $40) × 100 = 267.5%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 267.5% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the view that the unequal distribution of energy resources causes greater problems than the environmental costs of energy use.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Problems from unequal distribution:
• Importing countries (UK, Japan, Germany) face energy insecurity when supplies are disrupted.
• OPEC and Russia can use oil and gas as political leverage; Russia cut gas to Europe in 2022.
• Conflict in oil regions destabilises whole economies (1973 embargo, 2022 Ukraine invasion).
• Poorer importers pay highest share of GDP on energy bills.
Problems from environmental costs:
• Burning fossil fuels emits CO2, the main driver of climate change.
• Oil spills (Deepwater Horizon 2010) damage ecosystems for years.
• Mining and drilling scar landscapes and pollute water (Appalachian coal, Niger Delta oil).
• HEP dams flood communities (Three Gorges displaced 1.3 million people).
Mastering (7-8): both sides examined with named examples and a clear judgement (e.g. distribution causes short-term crises, environmental costs cause long-term harm). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one side covered well, other only mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination. [1-2]
SPaG (4): consistently accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with confident use of specialist terms. [4]

lessons.title: Energy Futures: Reducing Reliance on Fossil Fuels

before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Examine question on energy futures, examiners reward answers that combine three things: technical content (which renewables work where), economics (which are cheapest, who pays the transition costs) and values (what different groups prioritise). Use specific data — solar costs down 90%, UK wind 30% of electricity, tar-sands 3× CO₂ intensity. Generic statements about ‘going green’ will not score.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an unconventional fossil fuel?
A) Natural gas from a conventional well
B) Shale gas extracted by fracking
C) Onshore wind power
D) Solar photovoltaic
practice_questions.marks: B) Shale gas extracted by fracking. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'carbon footprint'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The total amount of greenhouse gases emitted directly or indirectly by an individual, organisation or activity.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'How much CO₂ a person or company produces.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways individuals can reduce their carbon footprint.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: cut meat consumption; choose low-carbon transport (cycle, train, electric car); fewer or no flights; insulate homes; switch electricity supplier to renewable tariff; reduce consumption of fast fashion. Mastering: two specific actions. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain why developing fossil-fuel resources in ecologically sensitive areas (e.g. tar sands, Arctic oil) is controversial.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: high CO₂ intensity (tar sands 3× conventional); damage to fragile habitats and Indigenous lands; risk of oil spills in harsh remote conditions; locks in fossil-fuel use just as transition is needed; benefits flow to TNCs and governments not to local people. Mastering: 2+ reasons developed. [4]

practice_questions.text: If global solar PV costs fell 90% from 2010 to 2024, and a 1 kW system cost $7,500 in 2010, calculate the 2024 cost. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 90% decrease means new price = 10% of $7,500 = $750. Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: $750 with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the costs and benefits of switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy in a developed country.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: benefits — cuts CO₂ emissions; reduces import dependence (UK gas was 50% from Norway in 2022); creates new jobs (UK offshore wind sector now employs 30,000+); improves air quality. Costs — high upfront capital; intermittency requires storage; fossil-fuel jobs lost; some communities oppose wind farms; rare metals for batteries cause new environmental issues. Conclusion: long-run benefits outweigh short-term costs but transition must be planned with affected workers. Mastering (7–8): both costs and benefits, named examples and figures.

before.content_html:
A Different Kind of Question

The Edexcel B the people-and-environment unit paper ends with a 12-mark decision-making essay. You are given a resources booklet — maps, graphs, statistics, photographs, quotes — about a geographical issue drawn from Topics 7–9. You must choose between three proposed solutions and justify your choice. There is no ‘correct’ answer; what counts is the quality of your reasoning. Top-band answers do four things: weigh costs and benefits, use evidence from the booklet, balance opposing views, and reach a clearly justified conclusion.

Reading the Resources

Spend 5–7 minutes reading the booklet before writing. Annotate it. For each resource, ask: what does this tell me? and which option does it support?. Look for quantitative data (graphs, percentages, costs, numbers of people affected) — concrete numbers strengthen arguments. Look for qualitative data (quotes, photographs) — these capture human and environmental impacts. Look for spatial information on maps — which areas are at risk, which gain.

Key Fact

The 12-mark decision essay rewards specific evidence from the booklet. Citing ‘Figure 3 shows that the protected area covers 1,200 km²’ scores; vague references to ‘the resources’ do not.

Weighing Options

Each option in a decision essay has a mix of advantages and disadvantages, often analysed using cost-benefit analysis. The best answers think across three dimensions: economic (cost, jobs, GDP impact, who pays), environmental (CO₂, biodiversity, pollution, land-use change) and social (people affected, equity, displacement, cultural value). A solution that wins on cost may lose on environment; a solution that protects the environment may displace people. Knowing this in advance helps you write a balanced answer instead of just picking one option and dismissing the others.

Stakeholders and Perspectives

Different groups have different interests. Stakeholders are people, organisations or communities affected by a decision. In a rainforest decision, stakeholders might include: Indigenous peoples (traditional rights and livelihood), small-scale farmers (need land), logging companies (profit), national governments (development goals), Indigenous-rights NGOs (advocacy), climate scientists (carbon stock), tourists (ecotourism revenue). Listing the stakeholders and what each wants prevents you from defaulting to a one-sided answer.

Imagine the booklet asks you to choose between three Amazon strategies: (1) Open the rainforest to commercial logging with strict quotas. (2) Make the entire region a protected national park. (3) Promote ecotourism while keeping selective small-scale logging. Option 1 brings short-term jobs but long-term forest loss and CO₂ release. Option 2 protects biodiversity and carbon stocks but blocks economic development; risks illegal incursion if not enforced. Option 3 balances economic and environmental aims, gives Indigenous communities a stake, but is slower and harder to scale. A justified conclusion might pick option 3 with reasoning: ecotourism aligns Indigenous, environmental and economic interests — but only if backed by enforcement and infrastructure.

Structuring the Essay

A strong 12-mark decision essay has six paragraphs. Paragraph 1: state your decision and preview your reasons. Paragraph 2: option A — advantages with evidence. Paragraph 3: option A — disadvantages. Paragraphs 4–5: same treatment for option B and option C. Paragraph 6: justified conclusion that explicitly contrasts the chosen option with the alternatives. Aim for around 350–450 words. Reference at least three booklet sources by figure number or title (‘Figure 4 shows…’).

Key Fact

Top-band 12-mark answers (10–12 marks) explicitly compare the chosen option with the rejected ones. Saying ‘option B is best’ without showing why options A and C are weaker drops you to mid-band.

Common Pitfalls

Five common ways students lose marks: (1) summarising rather than evaluating — just describing the resources scores low. (2) One-sided answers that ignore costs of the chosen option. (3) No specific evidence — vague references to ‘the figures’ instead of named numbers. (4) No clear decision at the end — the question demands one. (5) Generic answers not rooted in the specific issue. Practising past papers across rainforest, energy and biosphere topics builds the muscle for choosing fast.

The decision essay can also draw on what you learned in Components 1 and 2. A question on tropical rainforests might invite you to use ideas from the global issues unit (climate change, hazards) or the UK issues unit (UK fieldwork on environmental quality). Examiners reward students who weave wider knowledge into the answer — for example noting that Amazon deforestation feeds climate change, which then increases UK flood risk — but only when it strengthens the argument, not as a tangent.
